title: Quiz: Measurement System Analysis — Gauge R&R

questions.text: A Gauge R&R study finds % GR&R = 35%. What does this mean?
options: 35% of total variation comes from the measurement system — it is unacceptable
questions.explanation: % GR&R > 30% means over 30% of total observed variation is caused by the measurement system itself. This is unacceptable — the measurement system must be improved before trusting any quality data.

questions.text: What is the difference between repeatability and reproducibility in a Gauge R&R study?
options: Repeatability is operator variation; reproducibility is equipment variation
Repeatability is how consistent the gauge is for one operator; reproducibility is how consistent results are across different operators
They are the same concept measured at different times
Repeatability applies to attribute data; reproducibility applies to variables data
questions.explanation: Repeatability (EV) = same operator, same part, same gauge — how consistent is the equipment? Reproducibility (AV) = different operators, same part — how much do operators differ from each other?

questions.text: A high % GR&R is especially harmful in Big Data contexts because it means sensors and data collection scripts introduce systematic variation that contaminates downstream analyses.
questions.explanation: In Big Data, the 'gauge' is often a sensor or API. High GR&R means a large fraction of variation in the data comes from the measurement system, not the process. This can mislead models, dashboards, and control charts.

questions.text: The Number of Distinct Categories (ndc) in a Gauge R&R study should be:
questions.explanation: ndc ≥ 5 indicates the measurement system can distinguish at least 5 distinct categories of parts. Fewer than 5 means the gauge cannot reliably detect differences between parts.

questions.text: The standard crossed Gauge R&R study design uses 10 parts, 2–3 operators, and 2–3 measurements per part per operator.
questions.explanation: The standard AIAG-recommended design is 10 parts × 3 operators × 3 replicates = 90 total measurements. This design allows estimation of both repeatability and reproducibility with adequate statistical power.
